advances: Every structural conclusion of the quadratic entropy-selection theorem 57c57a5fe0d4d1cc holds for every finite globally strictly convex target cost. In particular, adaptive selection of a strictly convex exposed face preserves complete row supports, convex-admissible assignment-share potentials, globally extendable integer-mean rows, and domination of original barycentric logarithmic costs by row costs. The strict Jensen tests of c300e9d112cefeb0 are sufficient exact finite input data.
author: research-agent
proof:
First, the extension of \(p=w/W\) is globally log-concave, agrees with all lattice values, and is finite-valued. The completeness and convex-admissibility conclusions at the start of 488f0a583886b5fc therefore apply in precisely the displayed normalization. In particular, every positive convex representation of an integral point in \(P\) gives a member of \(D\), and the logarithms of \(p\) obey the corresponding concavity inequality.

The diagonal array belongs to \(\mathcal F(p)\), and every coordinate of a feasible array lies in the finite interval \([0,p_{\mathbf I}]\). Thus the feasible set is a nonempty compact convex polytope. Since \(F\) is finite at each of the finitely many targets, \(V_F\) is a finite linear functional. Its minimizing set is a nonempty compact convex face. For each coordinate of \(\mathcal T_F\), choose one minimizing array positive there, and average these finitely many arrays. Denote this average by \(r^\circ\). It is minimizing, positive at every coordinate of \(\mathcal T_F\), and zero elsewhere. Its positive row targets are exactly \(\mathcal J_F\).

Suppose an integral \(\mathbf K\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal J_F)\) has a positive representation \(\mathbf K=\sum_{\mathbf J\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf J}\mathbf J\) in which at least one target differs from \(\mathbf K\). Completeness gives \(\mathbf K\in D\). Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\varepsilon\lambda_{\mathbf J}\le q_{\mathbf J}(r^\circ)\) for each used row. From each such row remove the subrow

\[
\varepsilon\lambda_{\mathbf J}\,
\frac{r^\circ_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{q_{\mathbf J}(r^\circ)}
\]

and add the sum of all removed subrows to row \(\mathbf K\). This preserves every column sum and nonnegativity. Each removed subrow has mean \(\mathbf J\); the sum has mass \(\varepsilon\) and mean \(\mathbf K\). Thus all row moment identities are also preserved, including if \(\mathbf K\) is one of the removed targets. The decrease in objective is

\[
\varepsilon\left[\sum_{\mathbf J\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf J}F(\mathbf J)-F(\mathbf K)\right]>0.
\]

The inequality is strict finite Jensen inequality: the positively weighted points are not all equal. It contradicts minimality. A lattice point in the hull outside \(\mathcal J_F\) would admit just such a representation. A member of \(\mathcal J_F\) that was not a vertex would admit such a representation using other members. This proves both hull assertions. This is the only part of the proof that requires strict convexity of the target cost.

For the intrinsic cardinality bound, fix \(\mathbf J_0\in\mathcal J_F\) and let

\[
\mathscr L=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal J_F-\mathbf J_0)\cap\mathbb Z^n.
\]

Its real span has dimension \(k\): it is contained in the displayed subspace and contains the differences that span that subspace. Every subgroup of \(\mathbb Z^n\) has an integer basis that is real-linearly independent. An elementary induction proves this. If its first-coordinate image is nonzero, that image is \(a\mathbb Z\) for a least positive \(a\); choose a subgroup element with first coordinate \(a\). Subtracting its integer multiples leaves the subgroup with first coordinate zero, to which the induction hypothesis in \(\mathbb Z^{n-1}\) applies. The chosen element together with that basis is an integer basis and is real-linearly independent. If the first-coordinate image is zero, apply the induction directly to the remaining coordinates. Applied to \(\mathscr L\), its basis has \(k\) elements, so \(\mathscr L/2\mathscr L\) has \(2^k\) classes. Two distinct targets in the same class have an integral midpoint. The merging argument would then strictly improve the objective. Hence there is at most one target in each class, proving \(|\mathcal J_F|\le2^k\), including \(k=0\).

We prove a strict dual characterization of the entire minimizing face for this cost. Flatten the array coordinates as \(e=(\mathbf J,\mathbf I)\), write the column and row moment equalities as \(\mathsf A r=b\), and set \(c_e=F(\mathbf J)\). All redundant equations may remain. Write \(\mathcal Z_F=(D\times D)\setminus\mathcal T_F\). A vector \(h\) supported on \(\mathcal T_F\) with \(\mathsf A h=0\) allows both perturbations \(r^\circ\pm th\) for small \(t>0\). Optimality gives \(c\cdot h=0\). The orthogonal-complement identity for a finite matrix therefore supplies a finite vector \(y_0\) with

\[
c_{\mathcal T_F}=\mathsf A_{\mathcal T_F}^{\mathsf T}y_0.
\]

If \(\mathcal Z_F\) is empty, this already gives the dual used below. Otherwise define \(s^0_{\mathcal Z_F}=c_{\mathcal Z_F}-\mathsf A_{\mathcal Z_F}^{\mathsf T}y_0\) and the compact set

\[
\mathcal Q=\left\{z\ge0\text{ on }\mathcal Z_F:
\sum_e z_e=1,\quad
\mathsf A_{\mathcal Z_F}z\in\operatorname{range}(\mathsf A_{\mathcal T_F})\right\}.
\]

For any \(z\in\mathcal Q\), choose \(h_{\mathcal T_F}\) with \(\mathsf A_{\mathcal T_F}h_{\mathcal T_F}=-\mathsf A_{\mathcal Z_F}z\), and set \(h_{\mathcal Z_F}=z\). Small positive perturbations \(r^\circ+th\) are feasible. Their objective increment divided by \(t\) is \(s^0_{\mathcal Z_F}\cdot z\). It is nonnegative by optimality, and cannot be zero: that would give a minimizing array positive at a coordinate of \(\mathcal Z_F\). Thus it is strictly positive. If \(\mathcal Q\) is nonempty, compactness gives \(\delta=\min_{z\in\mathcal Q}s^0_{\mathcal Z_F}\cdot z>0\), and choose \(\epsilon=\delta/2\). If \(\mathcal Q\) is empty, choose \(\epsilon=1\).

Put \(c'=c-\epsilon\mathbf1_{\mathcal Z_F}\), with the indicator zero on \(\mathcal T_F\). For every \(h\) satisfying \(\mathsf A h=0\) and \(h_{\mathcal Z_F}\ge0\), one has \(c'\cdot h\ge0\). If \(h_{\mathcal Z_F}=0\), the value is zero by the row-space identity. Otherwise its positive coordinate sum \(a\) gives \(h_{\mathcal Z_F}/a\in\mathcal Q\), and

\[
c'\cdot h=a\left(s^0_{\mathcal Z_F}\cdot\frac{h_{\mathcal Z_F}}a-\epsilon\right)\ge a(\delta-\epsilon)>0.
\]

This latter case is impossible if \(\mathcal Q\) is empty.

Consider the convex cone

\[
\mathcal C_{\mathrm{dual}}=
\left\{\mathsf A^{\mathsf T}y+s:
s_{\mathcal T_F}=0,\ s_{\mathcal Z_F}\ge0\right\}.
\]

It is closed. Indeed, it is generated by a finite basis of \(\operatorname{range}(\mathsf A^{\mathsf T})\), the negatives of that basis, and the coordinate vectors indexed by \(\mathcal Z_F\). Any conic representation can be reduced to linearly independent positive-support generators: if those generators are dependent, subtract a signed dependence, with sign chosen to have a positive coefficient, until a positive coefficient first vanishes. Repeat. For a convergent sequence of conic combinations, pass to a subsequence using the same independent subset, of which there are only finitely many. Its coefficients converge by the continuous linear inverse on their span, and their limits are nonnegative. Hence the limit belongs to the cone.

If \(c'\) were outside this closed cone, let \(u_0\) be its closest point in the cone. Existence follows from a bounded minimizing sequence. Differentiating squared distance along segments gives \( (c'-u_0)\cdot(u-u_0)\le0\) for every cone point \(u\). Taking \(u=0,2u_0\) gives \( (c'-u_0)\cdot u_0=0\). Thus \(h=u_0-c'\) satisfies \(h\cdot u\ge0\) throughout the cone and

\[
h\cdot c'=-\|c'-u_0\|^2<0.
\]

Because the cone contains \(\operatorname{range}(\mathsf A^{\mathsf T})\) with both signs and every coordinate vector indexed by \(\mathcal Z_F\), these inequalities imply \(\mathsf A h=0\) and \(h_{\mathcal Z_F}\ge0\). This contradicts the preceding paragraph. Therefore \(c'\) belongs to the cone. Adding back \(\epsilon\mathbf1_{\mathcal Z_F}\), or using \(y_0\) in the empty case, gives finite \(y,s\) such that

\[
c=\mathsf A^{\mathsf T}y+s,\qquad
s_e=0\ (e\in\mathcal T_F),\qquad
s_e>0\ (e\in\mathcal Z_F).
\]

For every feasible array, \(V_F(r)=b\cdot y+s\cdot r\), and \(V_F(r^\circ)=b\cdot y\). Thus the entire minimizing face consists exactly of the feasible arrays supported on \(\mathcal T_F\). This proof uses only that \(c\) is a finite cost vector, not that it is quadratic or convex.

Write the column multipliers of \(y\) as \(\alpha_{\mathbf I}\) and the row moment multipliers as \(\boldsymbol\eta_{\mathbf J}\). Define affine functions on the original \(\mathbb R^n\) by

\[
\ell_{\mathbf J}(x)=F(\mathbf J)-\boldsymbol\eta_{\mathbf J}\cdot(x-\mathbf J).
\]

The strict dual says \(\ell_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf I)=\alpha_{\mathbf I}\) exactly on \(\mathcal T_F\), and \(\ell_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf I)>\alpha_{\mathbf I}\) elsewhere. Every column has positive prescribed sum, so it has at least one permitted coordinate. Consequently \(\alpha_{\mathbf I}=\min_{\mathbf K\in D}\ell_{\mathbf K}(\mathbf I)\). Define the convex equality cell

\[
\Omega_{F,\mathbf J}=
\{x\in P:\ell_{\mathbf J}(x)\le\ell_{\mathbf K}(x)\text{ for all }\mathbf K\in D\}.
\]

For every positive row, \(D_{F,\mathbf J}=D\cap\Omega_{F,\mathbf J}\). Any integer point in its convex hull therefore belongs to \(P\cap\Omega_{F,\mathbf J}\cap\mathbb Z^n=D_{F,\mathbf J}\), proving completeness. The normalized positive row of \(r^\circ\) represents \(\mathbf J\) as a convex combination of \(D_{F,\mathbf J}\). Hence \(\mathbf J\in D_{F,\mathbf J}\). This argument includes cells in proper affine subspaces and cells on the boundary of \(P\).

Continuity of \(H\) gives an entropy maximizer on the compact minimizing face. For fixed \(p_{\mathbf I}>0\), the summand \(-t\log(t/p_{\mathbf I})\) is strictly concave on \([0,p_{\mathbf I}]\). For positive \(t\) its second derivative is \(-1/t\); if one endpoint is zero, the strict inequality follows directly from \(-t\log t\). The sum is therefore strictly concave on any nonconstant array segment, giving uniqueness of \(r_F\).

If this maximizer vanished at a permitted coordinate, mix it with \(r^\circ\). At the previously zero coordinates of \((1-t)r_F+tr^\circ\), the entropy increment is \(-t\log t\) times the strictly positive sum of the corresponding \(r^\circ\) entries, plus \(O(t)\). At the finitely many previously positive coordinates, differentiability gives an increment \(O(t)\). For sufficiently small positive \(t\), the total is positive, a contradiction. Off \(\mathcal T_F\), all minimizing arrays vanish. Thus its support is exactly \(\mathcal T_F\).

On this exact support, every \(h\) with \(\mathsf A h=0\) allows both small perturbations of \(r_F\), and the strict dual characterization keeps them on the minimizing face. Entropy stationarity and the finite row-space/kernel identity supply finite scalars \(a_{\mathbf I}\) and finite vectors \(\boldsymbol\gamma_{\mathbf J}\) with

\[
-\log\frac{r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{p_{\mathbf I}}-1
=a_{\mathbf I}+\boldsymbol\gamma_{\mathbf J}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)
\qquad((\mathbf J,\mathbf I)\in\mathcal T_F).
\]

Set \(\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf J}=-\boldsymbol\gamma_{\mathbf J}\). At each source define its nonempty active set and normalizing sum

\[
\mathcal A_F(\mathbf I)=\{\mathbf K:(\mathbf K,\mathbf I)\in\mathcal T_F\},\qquad
N_F(\mathbf I)=\sum_{\mathbf K\in\mathcal A_F(\mathbf I)}
e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf K}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf K)}.
\]

Exponentiation and summing the column determine the column factor exactly, giving

\[
r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=
p_{\mathbf I}\frac{e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf J}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)}}{N_F(\mathbf I)}
\quad((\mathbf J,\mathbf I)\in\mathcal T_F),
\qquad r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=0\quad\text{otherwise}.
\]

No forced-zero coordinate occurs in the denominator. Redundant moment equations and boundary rows do not affect this kernel argument.

Fix a row \(\mathbf J\in\mathcal J_F\) and a positive barycentric representation \(\mathbf z=\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n\), with \(E\subseteq D_{F,\mathbf J}\). Completeness gives \(\mathbf z\in D_{F,\mathbf J}\). If \(\mathbf K\in\mathcal A_F(\mathbf z)\), the affine difference \(\ell_{\mathbf K}-\ell_{\mathbf J}\) is nonnegative at each source in \(E\) and zero at \(\mathbf z\). Its positive weighted average is zero, so each source value is zero. The strict dual then gives

\[
\mathcal A_F(\mathbf z)\subseteq\bigcap_{\mathbf I\in E}\mathcal A_F(\mathbf I).
\]

For each \(\mathbf K\), affineness of the exponent gives

\[
e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf K}\cdot(\mathbf z-\mathbf K)}
=\prod_{\mathbf I\in E}
\left(e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf K}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf K)}\right)^{\lambda_{\mathbf I}}.
\]

Weighted Hölder on the common active set, followed by its inclusion at each source, yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_F(\mathbf z)
&\le\prod_{\mathbf I\in E}
\left(\sum_{\mathbf K\in\mathcal A_F(\mathbf z)}
e^{\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf K}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf K)}\right)^{\lambda_{\mathbf I}}\\
&\le\prod_{\mathbf I\in E}N_F(\mathbf I)^{\lambda_{\mathbf I}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For completeness, the first inequality follows by dividing each positive source family on that common set by its sum. Weighted arithmetic-geometric mean bounds the product of its normalized entries by their weighted arithmetic mean for each \(\mathbf K\); summing over \(\mathbf K\) bounds the resulting sum by one. No locally constant active-set assumption is used.

The exact entropy formula gives

\[
\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf I)
=\log N_F(\mathbf I)-\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathbf J}\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf J).
\]

Taking logarithms of the preceding bound and subtracting this affine function proves convex-admissibility of the share potential. Global log-concavity of \(p\) gives \(\log p_{\mathbf z}\ge\sum\lambda_{\mathbf I}\log p_{\mathbf I}\). Subtracting the share inequality from this proves the asserted concavity inequality for the row logarithms.

To construct the global row extension, set \(P_{F,\mathbf J}=\operatorname{conv}(D_{F,\mathbf J})\) and take on this hull the lower convex roof of the finite values \(-\log r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}\). Explicitly, at each \(x\) minimize their coefficient-weighted sum over nonnegative coefficients of sum one and barycenter \(x\). The coefficient set is a nonempty compact subset of a finite simplex, so the roof is finite and attained. Combining minimizing coefficient vectors proves convexity. The row logarithm inequality just established at every integral barycenter says that every such representation at a site \(\mathbf I\) has objective at least \(-\log r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}\); the singleton representation attains that value. Thus the roof agrees exactly with every row value. Its negative exponential on \(P_{F,\mathbf J}\), extended by zero elsewhere in \(\mathbb R^n\), is finite-valued and globally log-concave. If both endpoints are in the hull, this follows from convexity of the roof; otherwise the right side of the log-concavity inequality is zero. Row completeness ensures agreement with every lattice zero. This is the roof mechanism of 488f0a583886b5fc with the row normalization map stated above. The same construction applied to \(\psi_{F,\mathbf J}\) gives a finite convex extension of the share values on the row hull. Division by \(q_{F,\mathbf J}>0\) preserves global log-concavity, and the row moment equation gives mean \(\mathbf J\).

Finally, any component at \(\mathbf J\) inside this row support has \(\mathbf J\) itself in the positive support. Direct subtraction gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_\lambda(r_{F,\mathbf J,\cdot})-G_\lambda(p)
&=\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf I)
-\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf J)\\
&\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The original cost is nonnegative by global log-concavity of \(p\). A common positive scale cancels in \(G_\lambda\), proving both equalities under normalization and all cost assertions for the original \(w\). This applies to arbitrary positive barycentric representations, so it includes every relevant member of the original finite families \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\).

For the finite-data version, part 1 of accepted fact c300e9d112cefeb0 states exactly that the displayed strict tests are equivalent to restriction of a finite globally strictly convex function, and supplies a globally strongly convex exact extension. Choose that extension for \(F\). Since the array objective depends only on its values on \(D\), its entire minimizing face, entropy maximizer, rows, and all proved conclusions are exactly those for the original vector \(f\). Conversely, any given strictly convex \(F\) satisfies those tests by strict Jensen. This proves the claimed equivalence without changing any capacities or perturbing the selected face.

The proof has checked each use of the old quadratic objective. Strict target merging uses strict Jensen in place of the quadratic variance identity. The strict dual, convex equality cells, entropy stationarity, active-set inclusion, Hölder inequality, roof extension, and original-cost comparison use only finiteness of the target cost and the given table's log-concavity. Thus every listed structural conclusion of 57c57a5fe0d4d1cc transfers exactly to the adaptive strictly convex cost setting.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\), and let \(w=(w_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}\) be any globally extendable finite table in the sense of accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc. Thus \(w\not\equiv0\), its positive support \(D\) is finite, and there is a finite-valued globally log-concave extension agreeing with every lattice value, including every zero. Retain its original mass \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}>0\), complete support \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), and canonical normalization

\[
p_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}/W,\qquad
\phi_{\mathbf I}=\log\frac{w_{\max}}{w_{\mathbf I}}
=\log\frac{p_{\max}}{p_{\mathbf I}},\qquad
B=\max_{\mathbf I\in D}\phi_{\mathbf I}.
\]

Write \(P=\operatorname{conv}(D)\). The passage \(w\mapsto p\) does not change \(D,\phi,B\), or any barycentric logarithmic cost. When \(w\) is the original fiber table of a convex body, the locked \(n,d,C,S,W,h_S\) keep their original meanings. In particular \(W=\mathcal H_d(S)\); no new body or integer lattice chart is introduced.

Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite everywhere and globally strictly convex. Use the feasible arrays and conditional assignment entropy of 57c57a5fe0d4d1cc, with the adaptive-cost convention of c300e9d112cefeb0:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(p)&=\left\{r\ge0:
\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\ (\mathbf I\in D),\quad
\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)=\mathbf0\ (\mathbf J\in D)
\right\},\\
q_{\mathbf J}(r)&=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I},\qquad
V_F(r)=\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}q_{\mathbf J}(r)F(\mathbf J),\\
H(r)&=-\sum_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
\log\frac{r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{p_{\mathbf I}},\qquad 0\log0=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(H(r)\) is conditional assignment entropy, as in those accepted facts; the target entropy \(S(q)\) of c300e9d112cefeb0 remains a different functional. Let \(\mathcal F_{\min}^F\) be the entire \(V_F\)-minimizing face, and define

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T_F&=\{(\mathbf J,\mathbf I):r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}>0
\text{ for some }r\in\mathcal F_{\min}^F\},\\
\mathcal J_F&=\{\mathbf J:(\mathbf J,\mathbf I)\in\mathcal T_F
\text{ for some }\mathbf I\},\\
D_{F,\mathbf J}&=\{\mathbf I:(\mathbf J,\mathbf I)\in\mathcal T_F\}
\qquad(\mathbf J\in\mathcal J_F).
\end{aligned}
\]

The subscripts map these objects exactly to \(\mathcal F_{\min},\mathcal T,\mathcal J,D_{\mathbf J}\) of 57c57a5fe0d4d1cc when \(F(x)=\|x\|^2\). There is a unique maximizer \(r_F\) of \(H\) on \(\mathcal F_{\min}^F\), and it is positive exactly on \(\mathcal T_F\). Its target law is \(q_F=q(r_F)\), in the notation of c300e9d112cefeb0. With \(k=\dim\operatorname{aff}(\mathcal J_F)\),

\[
\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal J_F)\cap\mathbb Z^n=\mathcal J_F,
\qquad
\text{every member of }\mathcal J_F\text{ is a vertex of its hull},
\qquad
|\mathcal J_F|\le2^k\le2^n.
\]

For every \(\mathbf J\in\mathcal J_F\), its complete positive row support satisfies

\[
D_{F,\mathbf J}=\operatorname{conv}(D_{F,\mathbf J})\cap\mathbb Z^n,
\qquad \mathbf J\in D_{F,\mathbf J}.
\]

The assignment-share values

\[
\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf I)
=-\log\frac{r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{p_{\mathbf I}}
\qquad(\mathbf I\in D_{F,\mathbf J})
\]

are convex-admissible on this complete support. More explicitly, for every finite nonempty \(E\subseteq D_{F,\mathbf J}\), every positive coefficients \(\lambda_{\mathbf I}\) of sum one, and every integral barycenter \(\mathbf z=\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\mathbf I\),

\[
\mathbf z\in D_{F,\mathbf J},\qquad
\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf z)
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\psi_{F,\mathbf J}(\mathbf I),\qquad
\log r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf z}
\ge\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\log r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}.
\]

Consequently the row, with zero at every other lattice point, has a finite-valued globally log-concave extension. The row probability table

\[
u^{[\mathbf J]}_{\mathbf I}=r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}/q_{F,\mathbf J}
\]

is globally extendable, has complete support \(D_{F,\mathbf J}\), and has mean \(\mathbf J\). To apply 488f0a583886b5fc to this row, the precise map is \(w^{[\mathbf J]}=u^{[\mathbf J]}\), \(W^{[\mathbf J]}=1\), \(D^{[\mathbf J]}=D_{F,\mathbf J}\), and

\[
\phi^{[\mathbf J]}_{\mathbf I}
=\log\frac{\max_{\mathbf K\in D_{F,\mathbf J}}u^{[\mathbf J]}_{\mathbf K}}
{u^{[\mathbf J]}_{\mathbf I}}.
\]

This row potential is distinguished from both the original \(\phi\) and the share potential \(\psi_{F,\mathbf J}\); the original \(B\) is never replaced by a row maximum.

Retain exactly the barycentric families \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) and canonical costs \(G_E\) of 488f0a583886b5fc. For an arbitrary positive barycentric component \(\lambda\) at \(\mathbf J\in\mathcal J_F\) supported inside \(D_{F,\mathbf J}\), put

\[
G_\lambda(v)=\log v_{\mathbf J}-\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\log v_{\mathbf I}
\]

for any table \(v\) positive on those sites. This equals the canonical \(G_E\) when the component belongs to \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) and \(v=w\). Then

\[
0\le G_\lambda(w)=G_\lambda(p)
\le G_\lambda(r_{F,\mathbf J,\cdot})
=G_\lambda(u^{[\mathbf J]}).
\]

All conclusions hold for boundary targets, lower affine rank, rank zero, forced-zero entries, and components that are affinely dependent. The original integral quantities \(m_{\log}\) and \(\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}\) keep their definitions from 488f0a583886b5fc, including equality atoms and vertical normals. The fractional full-occurrence scores \(P_d,\mathcal B_d\) are not identified with integral hitting.

Equivalently, the theorem applies to any finite cost vector \(f=(f_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in D}\) satisfying all the finite strict Jensen tests

\[
\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}f_{\mathbf I}-f_{\mathbf J}>0
\quad\bigl(\mathbf J\in D,\ E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\setminus\{\{\mathbf J\}\}\bigr),
\]

with \(V_F\) replaced by \(V_f=\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}f_{\mathbf J}\). These are the exact cone conditions of c300e9d112cefeb0. No differentiability or strong-convexity modulus of the given \(F\) is required.
